# A paid preference for Lucky Charms {#sec-recommendations}

Consider a fictional assistant that knows the relevant cereal facts and
correctly evaluates products against a user's preferences. The example makes
no claim about Lucky Charms, its manufacturer, or any existing assistant.
Let $u(x,a)$ be the legitimate user-benefit score of product $a$ in situation
$x$, including the user's stated dietary and price constraints. The competent
policy chooses a feasible product maximizing $u$.

A sponsor-serving policy can instead choose
$$
a_b(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\text{ feasible}}
\bigl[u(x,a)+b\,t(x)\,\mathbf{1}\{a=\text{Lucky Charms}\}\bigr],
\qquad b>0.
$$
Suppose the unique user-optimal cereal beats Lucky Charms by $\Delta>0$,
and Lucky Charms is also feasible. When $t(x)=1$, a bonus $b>\Delta$ makes
Lucky Charms the unique choice. The factual database, preference understanding,
scoring machinery, and ability to explain real product attributes can remain intact. The deviation
is an undisclosed sponsor preference in a system represented as serving the
user. A disclosed advertisement, or a genuine user preference for the brand,
would be a different specification.

Here the incremental description includes the brand identifier, bonus,
trigger, and score adjustment. Their small size is plausible when the model
already represents products and scores; no particular neural parameter count
is established. Natural-language trigger recognition must be counted if it
is not already available. The example shows why truthful facts and competent
reasoning do not by themselves determine whose interests a recommendation
serves.

The trigger could simply select cereal recommendations, making broad factual
testing irrelevant to the deviation. The exponential sampling bound applies
only if the chosen evaluation distribution makes the trigger that rare; it
does not follow automatically for this commercial example. Frequent sponsored
choices could be readily detectable by a focused recommendation audit.
